analysis.one_liner: Slashes power plant emissions of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and global warming pollutants.
analysis.headline: The Clean Power Act of 2007 was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 2007 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written strict limits into the Clean Air Act for four pollutants from large power plants: sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (which cause acid rain and smog), mercury (a nerve toxin), and carbon dioxide and other global warming pollutants. It set a cap-and-trade system for those emissions, with most carbon allowances auctioned off over time and the money directed to households, energy efficiency, and clean energy. It also required utilities to get a growing share of power from renewables and to cut customers' electricity use, and required new plants to eventually match the emissions of an efficient natural gas plant.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people gain the most: less acid rain, smog, and mercury means fewer asthma attacks, contaminated fish, and ecosystem damage, and the bill's ratepayer protection section blocks most new conventional coal plants from passing their compliance costs through to electricity bills [S2] [S3]. The bill also directs allowance auction proceeds to households, communities hit by the transition, and low-income and minority communities, and funds energy-efficiency programs that reduce customers' bills [S3]. Renewable energy and natural gas generators gain a guaranteed and growing market: a renewable portfolio standard rising to 20% by 2020 and a rule that new baseload plants must eventually meet natural gas-level emission rates [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps national power plant emissions of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury at levels roughly half or less of prior levels, and creates an allowance system for compliance, cutting acid rain, smog, and mercury contamination [S2] [S3].

Sets declining national limits on global warming pollutants from power plants — down from 2.3 billion metric tons CO2-equivalent in 2011 to 1.5 billion by 2025 — and requires that if Congress fails to pass an economy-wide climate bill, power plant limits automatically tighten at least 3% per year from 2026 through 2050 [S3].

Requires 100% of carbon emission allowances to be auctioned within 15 years, with proceeds directed to households, transition-affected workers and communities, energy efficiency, and consumer rebates, rather than handed free to polluters [S3].

Bars owners of conventional coal plants entering operation after January 1, 2009 from recovering greenhouse gas compliance costs through their authorized electricity rates unless regulators find no feasible alternative [S3].

Requires a national renewable electricity standard rising from 5% in 2008 to 20% by 2020, plus mandatory utility energy-efficiency programs targeting reductions in peak demand and electricity use [S2] [S3].

Requires every coal plant with 50 megawatts or more to conduct public ambient air monitoring for sulfur dioxide and hazardous pollutants within a 30-mile radius, and makes all facility emission reports public [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal-fired power plant owners and operators bear the cost of installing pollution controls, buying emission allowances, and eventually shutting or retrofitting plants that cannot meet the limits; coal mining companies face shrinking demand for their product [S2] [S3]. Electricity customers could see higher rates in regions that rely on coal, though the bill restricts new conventional coal plants from passing compliance costs to ratepayers and provides transition assistance to affected workers and communities [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for coal-heavy utilities could raise electricity prices, which fall hardest on lower-income households and on electricity-intensive manufacturers; the bill's own allocation factors direct the EPA to weigh job losses and international competitiveness of manufacturing [S3].

The bill leans on emission allowance trading, which environmental justice advocates have long criticized because it can concentrate pollution around the plants that buy allowances rather than clean up; the bill responds with local-impact studies and authority to impose additional reductions, but the trading system remains the core compliance method [S2] [S3].

Coal miners and coal-dependent communities would bear real transition costs; the bill offers transition assistance funded by allowance auctions but does not guarantee comparable replacement employment [S3].

It regulates only power plants above 25 megawatts, leaving smaller fossil-fuel generators and other sectors of the economy outside the cap unless Congress later passed a broader bill, which the bill itself contemplates [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and environmental benefits are large and well established: power plant pollution causes measurable asthma, mercury contamination, and acid rain damage, and the bill targets all four pollutants with declining caps and mostly auctioned allowances — a design that returns value to households rather than giving polluters free permits. The honest cost is real: electricity rates in coal-reliant regions would rise, and coal communities would lose jobs, which is why the bill includes ratepayer protections and transition assistance. Whether the compliance timetable was realistic depends on how fast carbon capture and clean energy technology matured, which the bill addresses by requiring National Academy of Sciences feasibility reviews and allowing adjustments if requirements are technologically infeasible.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, so it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernard Sanders introduced the Clean Power Act of 2007 on April 24, 2007, joined by Sen. Joseph Lieberman, Sen. Patrick Leahy, and Sen. Russell Feingold as cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction [S5].
The full action history shows no further activity — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote — through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].
Companion climate legislation in the same Congress also failed to become law, so no version of these power plant emission limits was enacted during this Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired power plant owners and coal mining companies are better off because the bill died: they avoided new emission limits, control costs, and allowance purchases, and continued operating under the older, looser Clean Air Act rules. Electricity customers in coal-reliant regions avoided near-term rate increases, but at the cost of continued exposure to sulfur dioxide, smog-forming nitrogen oxides, and mercury from power plants.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal utilities avoided new pollution limits

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Power Act of 2007 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Joseph Lieberman, Patrick Leahy, and Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it four cosponsors total.

against.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on April 24, 2007 and never reported it out, held no recorded markup on it, and never sent it to the floor during the 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five Senate supporters were Democrats or independents who caucused with Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in a Democratic-held committee without a vote, so no roll-call exists to show the full partisan split.

industries.note: The bill's core cost falls on coal plant owners, who would have to install controls for four pollutants or buy allowances, with new conventional coal plants barred from passing greenhouse gas compliance costs through to customers. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the public's interest in cleaner air [S2] [S3].

Falling demand for coal to burn for electricity would shrink the coal market over time, since the bill pushes generation toward renewables, natural gas, and low-carbon coal with capture. Coal communities were offered transition assistance from allowance auction proceeds [S3].

A national renewable portfolio standard rising to 20% by 2020 plus a renewable credit trading program create a guaranteed and growing market for wind, solar, geothermal, and biomass power. Cheaper, cleaner generation for consumers runs alongside the industry's gain [S2] [S3].

New baseload plants would have to meet the emission rate of a new combined-cycle natural gas unit, making efficient gas plants the compliance benchmark and favoring gas over conventional coal. This is cheaper generation for the public but raises fuel dependence on gas [S2] [S3].

The bill funds competitive grants for five geological carbon dioxide disposal demonstration projects and sets federal storage standards, channeling public money toward an unproven technology that would allow continued fossil generation. Its benefit to the public depends on whether carbon capture ever works at scale [S2] [S3].
